report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is supported for *prescription, purified cannabidiol* used **as add-on therapy** in children/adolescents with treatment-resistant Dravet syndrome. It does not establish that non-prescription CBD products are effective or interchangeable.

Two high-quality, double-blind randomized placebo-controlled trials found fewer convulsive seizures with cannabidiol plus usual antiseizure medicines:

- In the 120-participant trial (ages 2–18), median convulsive-seizure frequency fell **39%** with cannabidiol (20 mg/kg/day), versus **13%** with placebo over 14 weeks; adverse events were more frequent with cannabidiol.  
  https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28813226/
- A separate 199-child dose-ranging trial found reductions of **48.7%** (10 mg/kg/day) and **45.7%** (20 mg/kg/day), versus **26.9%** with placebo. The lower dose had better tolerability.  
  https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/2762458

A systematic review/meta-analysis specifically evaluating placebo-controlled trials also assessed cannabidiol as adjunctive Dravet treatment, supporting that this conclusion rests on more than one trial.  
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40263-020-00708-6

**Important qualification:** Benefit is meaningful on average but not seizure freedom for most patients, follow-up in the blinded trials was short, and treatment has material risks—notably sleepiness, diarrhea, reduced appetite, liver-enzyme elevations, and drug interactions (especially relevant to concomitant antiseizure drugs). FDA labeling indicates Epidiolex for Dravet-associated seizures from age 2 and requires clinical monitoring.  
https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2018/210365lbl.pdf
